name: Alan J. Perlis
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED: the ACM "CHRONOLOGICAL LISTING OF A.M. TURING AWARD WINNERS" names "(1966) Perlis, Alan J *" (https://amturing.acm.org/byyear.cfm) -- the roster URL, fetched with curl and a browser User-Agent; WebFetch 403s on amturing.acm.org. a1: born 1 April 1922 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania (ACM award-winner biography). a2: PhD, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, 1950, in mathematics -- dissertation "On integral equations, their solution by iteration and analytic continuation", advisor Philip Franklin; the MSc (MIT, 1949) and the BS in chemistry from Carnegie Institute of Technology precede it. ACM dates the BS 1942 (graduated with honours 20 December 1942) while Wikipedia says 1943; immaterial here because the PhD is the terminal credential. a3: Ballistic Research Laboratory, Aberdeen Proving Ground, Maryland, 1951, computing ballistics tables on ENIAC/EDVAC/ORDVAC -- first paid post in the computing domain per the ACM biography; Project Whirlwind (1952) and the Carnegie Institute of Technology faculty appointment (1956) follow. a4: UNKNOWN. SERIAL-FOUNDER CHECK: no company or venture founding found at any point -- the career is entirely academic and professional-society (ACM president 1962-64, first head of the Carnegie computer science department, Yale CS chair from 1971), so there is no earlier venture that could have crossed a bar first. a5: 1966. Per frame.md the anchor is the ANNOUNCEMENT year, not the prize's designated year; for the inaugural Turing Award the two coincide, because the award was presented and its Turing Lecture delivered inside the designated year: the ACM Digital Library record for Perlis's Turing lecture "The Synthesis of Algorithmic Systems" (JACM 14(1), January 1967, https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/321371.321372) gives its original venue as "ACM '66: Proceedings of the 1966 21st national conference". This is the opposite pattern to modern Turing Awards (cf. p128 Liskov, designated 2008 / announced 2009), where announcement runs a year behind. a6: unknown -- his later honours (AFIPS Education Award 1984, Computer Pioneer Award 1986) are outside the four enumerated prize families in frame.md.

name: Maurice V. Wilkes
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED: the ACM "CHRONOLOGICAL LISTING OF A.M. TURING AWARD WINNERS" names "(1967) Wilkes, Maurice V.*" (https://amturing.acm.org/byyear.cfm) -- the roster URL, fetched with curl and a browser User-Agent. a1: born 26 June 1913 in Dudley, English Midlands (ACM award-winner biography; Wikipedia agrees). a2: BOUNDED 1936-1937, both ends sourced, because two authoritative sources disagree by one year on the Cambridge PhD in physics (radio propagation of long waves in the ionosphere, advisor J. A. Ratcliffe). LOW END: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Wilkes states "in 1936 completed his PhD in physics". HIGH END: the ACM award-winner page's education line reads "BA (1934 - mathematics), MA (1936), PhD (1937 - physics) St Johns College, Cambridge University". Cambridge's own archived short biography (cl.cam.ac.uk/~mvw1/short-biography.html) gives no doctorate year at all, and computerhistory.org and britannica.com were fetched and yielded nothing on the point, so the disagreement is not resolvable on two genuine attempts and the honest record is the two-year bracket. Note the two sources also disagree on when he began research (ACM: research student at the Cavendish from October 1935; Cambridge short bio: graduate student from 1934), which is what generates the offset. a3: 1937 -- "In early 1937, the University set up a Computing Laboratory under the direction of Lennard-Jones, and Wilkes was appointed assistant director from October 1937" (ACM biography). CONFIDENCE medium because Wikipedia instead describes an undated "junior faculty position" at Cambridge from 1936; either way the first computing-domain appointment falls in 1936-1937 and 1937 is the dated one. a4: UNKNOWN. SERIAL-FOUNDER CHECK: no company founded. He was a founder MEMBER and first president of the British Computer Society (1957-60), which is a professional society, not a venture, and his later industry roles (Digital Equipment Corporation from 1980, Olivetti's Research Strategy Board from 1986, later AT&T and HP) were salaried positions in existing firms -- so no earlier commercial venture exists that could have crossed a bar before the prize. a5: 1967. Per frame.md the anchor is the ANNOUNCEMENT year; for the second Turing Award the award year and its Turing Lecture fall in the same calendar year, and ACM records him as "Turing Lecturer, Association for Computing Machinery, 1967" on the same award-winner page as the 1967 award (the ACM DL page for the lecture "Computers Then and Now", JACM 15(1) January 1968, returned only a stub to curl on two attempts, so the lecture's conference venue is not cited here; the 1967 designation itself rests on ACM's own byyear listing and award-winner page). Same-year pattern as p176 Perlis and the reverse of modern awards (cf. p128 Liskov). a6: unknown -- his later honours (Harry H. Goode Memorial Award 1968, Eckert-Mauchly Award 1980, Faraday Medal 1981, Kyoto Prize 1992) are all outside the four enumerated prize families in frame.md.

name: Lars Valerian Ahlfors
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED: the IMU Fields Medal laureates listing carries "1936 / Lars Valerian Ahlfors / Jesse Douglas" (https://www.mathunion.org/imu-awards/fields-medal) -- the roster URL, fetched with curl and a browser User-Agent. a1: born 18 April 1907 in Helsinki (Wikipedia, citing Boston Globe and Fresno Bee obituaries and the Biografiskt lexikon for Finland). a2: doctorate, University of Helsinki, 1930 -- thesis containing his proof of Denjoy's conjecture (MacTutor, St Andrews); he had entered Helsinki in 1924 and taken his first degree in 1928 under Lindelof and Nevanlinna, so 1930 is the terminal credential. Wikipedia independently states "He completed his doctorate from the University of Helsinki in 1930", so both sources agree -- unlike p177 Wilkes. a3: 1930, lecturer in mathematics at the Swedish-language Abo Akademi in Turku, taken up directly after the doctorate (MacTutor); Wikipedia says only that he "began his academic career at Abo Akademi" without a year, and dates the Helsinki adjunct/associate professorship to 1933, which MacTutor confirms. a4: UNKNOWN. SERIAL-FOUNDER CHECK: no company or venture at any point -- a purely academic career (Abo Akademi, Helsinki, Harvard from autumn 1936, ETH Zurich 1945, Harvard again 1946-1977). a5: 1936, the announcement year and the designated year alike. The inaugural Fields Medals were conferred at the International Congress of Mathematicians in Oslo in 1936, and MacTutor records that Ahlfors "was told only hours before the ceremony" -- so the recognition landed in 1936 with no announcement/designation gap of the kind frame.md warns about. a6: unknown -- his later honours (Wihuri International Prize 1968, Wolf Prize in Mathematics 1981, Leroy P. Steele Prize 1982) fall outside the four enumerated prize families in frame.md, and he received only one Fields Medal.

name: Zach Sims
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED: the roster URL https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/codecademy is YC's own company page for Codecademy and names Zach Sims as founder; corroborated by Wikipedia, which dates the YC summer 2011 batch acceptance and the August 2011 founding. a1: born 1990 (Wikipedia infobox lede and category); no exact date published, hence medium. a2: UNKNOWN. Dropout: he entered Columbia University with the class of 2012 as a political science major and left in 2011, a year before graduation, so under the last-completed-credential rule the anchor would be his high-school diploma -- but no source found names his high school or a graduation year. Three attempts: Wikipedia wikitext (silent), a web search for his secondary schooling (nothing), and grokipedia.com/page/Zach_Sims plus the Columbia College feature at college.columbia.edu (both HTTP 403). Recorded unknown rather than back-computing 2008 from the class-of-2012 entry year, which would be an inferred date. a3: BOUNDED 2010-2011 at LOW confidence -- he worked for GroupMe, founded by his Columbia friend Jared Hecht, whom he approached after seeing GroupMe demoed at TechCrunch Disrupt in 2010 (Wikipedia, citing Business Insider); the demo year gives the lower end and his departure to run Codecademy full-time in summer 2011 the upper end, but no source gives a start date. a4: 2011 -- Codecademy founded August 2011 with Ryan Bubinski (Wikipedia). SERIAL-FOUNDER CHECK: NO earlier venture found. The only earlier commercial activity on record is emailing manufacturers at age 13 about a waterproof iPod case, which was an idea and not a company; GroupMe was Jared Hecht's company, where Sims was an employee, not a co-founder. Codecademy is therefore both the first venture and the hit entity. a5: BOUNDED 2016-2018 rev10, constant-2026-dollar bars from src.cpi. UPPER END, hard figure: Skillsoft's 22 December 2021 investor presentation (filed as part of DEFA14A, SEC accession 0001104659-21-152436) prints Codecademy's revenue history as $11M (2018), $19M (2019), $33M (2020), $43M (2021E). The 2018 rev10 bar is $7,799,735, so $11M clears it by 41% -- margin comfortably over 20%. The 2020 and 2021 figures are independently confirmed by Codecademy's audited statements of operations (Ryzac, Inc. d.b.a. Codecademy, revenue net $32,841,335 for 2020 and $41,853,306 for 2021, Skillsoft 8-K/A EX-99.1, accession 0001558370-22-010154), which match the deck to within rounding and establish the deck as reliable. LOWER END, QUALITATIVE -- FLAGGED: no dollar figure exists for 2016 or 2017. TechCrunch's 12 July 2016 report on the $30M Naspers round is headlined "Codecademy, the free online coding school" and states the company "is already generating some revenue from a paid 'professional' service ... (and costs about $20 per month)" -- a company at the very start of monetising, which places 2016 revenue below that year's $7,454,953 bar; the paid Pro tier proper was only released on 3 August 2017 (TechCrunch, via Wikipedia). So the crossing falls in 2017 or 2018 and the honest bracket is 2016-2018. This is a row where a qualitative scale claim is doing the dating work at the low end. The frame's founding-year fallback would give the much wider and equally valid 2011-2018; the narrower bracket is used because the 2016 monetisation evidence is specific and the 2018 figure is only $11M, which leaves no room for 2016 to have been above $7.45M. The IPO/acq50 fallback is BARRED here: revenue is documented from after the crossing and the $525M Skillsoft acquisition is years late. a6: 2021 -- Skillsoft agreed on 22 December 2021 to acquire Codecademy for approximately $525 million, the event that made the company what it is known for; the deal closed 5 April 2022.

name: Larry Page
notes: LIST MEMBERSHIP CONFIRMED: the roster URL https://www.forbes.com/profile/larry-page/ was fetched with curl and a browser User-Agent and names Larry Page with an embedded Person record (net worth $281,857,085,000), the label "Billionaires - position 2", and a printed Self-Made Score of 8 -- inside the roster's 6-10 self-made band. a1: born 26 March 1973 in Lansing, Michigan (Wikipedia). a2: 1998, MS in computer science, Stanford University, cited by Wikipedia to Stanford School of Engineering's own alumni page; the BSE in computer engineering with honors from the University of Michigan (1995, cited to record.umich.edu and research.google) precedes it. NOT a dropout case in the usual sense: he enrolled in Stanford's CS PhD programme and never finished it, but the MS is a completed credential and is therefore the anchor, in line with the last-completed-credential rule. a3: 1998 -- JUDGMENT CALL, conf medium. No paid employment of any kind before Google is documented anywhere: he went from the Michigan BSE straight into the Stanford PhD programme, and BackRub/PageRank was dissertation research, i.e. education, not a job. Following the study's existing precedent that a founding can serve as first domain work where nothing earlier exists (p He Xiangjian, "a3/a4: 1968 ... founding counts as first domain work"), a3 is set equal to a4 at the 1998 incorporation, when he appointed himself CEO. a4: 1998 -- Brin and Page incorporated Google, Inc. (Wikipedia, citing about.google and Google's own management page; the Bechtolsheim $100,000 cheque made out to a company that did not yet exist is the well-known marker of the incorporation fortnight). SERIAL-FOUNDER CHECK: NO earlier venture. As a Michigan undergraduate he built a Lego inkjet printer, proposed a personal rapid-transit system for the campus, and "developed a business plan for a company that would use software to build a music synthesizer" (Fortune, via Wikipedia) -- a business plan, never an incorporated or trading company, and no revenue is claimed for any of them. Google is both the first venture and the hit entity. a5: 2000, PINNED (not bounded), rev10, primary basis. Google's own Form S-1 of 29 April 2004 prints Selected Consolidated Financial Data with net revenues, in thousands, of $220 (1999), $19,108 (2000), $86,426 (2001), $347,848 (2002), $961,874 (2003). Constant-2026-dollar bars from src.cpi: the 1999 rev10 bar is $5,174,829 and 1999 revenue of $220,000 is 96% BELOW it; the 2000 bar is $5,348,773 and 2000 revenue of $19,108,000 is 257% ABOVE it. Both ends of the crossing are therefore sourced from the same audited table and the year is exact, with an enormous margin -- nothing near the 20% flag on either side. Note that a nominal $10M test would have dated this row 2001 instead of 2000, exactly the constant-dollar defect the brief warns about. The ipo fallback is BARRED and unnecessary: revenue is documented from before and after the crossing, and the August 2004 IPO is four years late. a6: 2004 -- the Form S-1 registering Google's initial public offering, which priced in August 2004 and is the point at which Google became the company he is known for.
